label: vgs
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{vgs} \item[{}]
\begin{itemize} \item[{{\rm$($a$)$}}]                                                                                             
The set $E:=\{(w_{i},k_{i})| 0 \le  i < m+n\}$, is the  equivalence class of $(w_0,k_0)$ in $[\mathtt{W}\times{\mathbb Z}]$. 
\item[{{\rm$($b$)$}}] The equivalence class of 
$(\stackrel{\rm o}{\mathfrak{b}}(w_0),k_0)$ in 
$[\stackrel{{\rm o}}{\mathcal{B}} \times {\mathbb Z}]$ is   $\{(\stackrel{\rm o}{\mathfrak{b}}(w_i),k_i))| 0 \le  i < m+n\}.$
\item[{{\rm$($c$)$}}]  If $0\le i \le j\le m+n$ and $k_i\equiv k_j \mod mn$ then $i=j$.
\item[{{\rm$($d$)$}}] If $(w_{i},k_{i})\in E$ and $m$ divides $k_i - k_0$, then $\sum_{j=1}^{i}c_j$ equals $ 0 $ or $m$. 
\item[{{\rm$($e$)$}}] If $w_0= \mathtt{x}\mathtt{r}$  for some word $\mathtt{x}$, $(w_{i},k_{i})\in E$ and $m$ divides $k_i - k_0$, then $\sum_{j=1}^{i}c_j=0$. 
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If the first letter in $w_i$ is $\mathtt{r}$, then $\lambda_{i+1}=\lambda_{i}^{-_\mathtt{c}}$ and 
$(w_{i},k_{i}) \sim (w_{i+1},k_{i}+n)$ by \eqref{2kr} and this agrees with \eqref{ips}.
Thus $E$ is contained the equivalence class of $(w_0,k_0)$.  However the set $E$ is closed under the basic instances (\eqref{1kr} and \eqref{2kr}) of $\sim$, so the equivalence class can be no larger.  This shows (a) and the proof of (b)  is similar.   Note that  (c)  and (d) follow from \eqref{ips}. If $w_0= \mathtt{x}\mathtt{r}$, then $ c_{m+n} =1$  and  $k_0= k_{m+n} =  k_{m+n-1} +n $, so $m$ cannot divide $k_i - k_0$, unless $\sum_{j=1}^{i}c_j=0$.

label: glk
title: Example
body_md:
\label{glk}{\rm If  ${\lambda= \boldsymbol \lambda},$ then  $w=\mathtt{w}(\lambda)=\mathtt{r}^{}  \mathtt{d}^{n-1}\mathtt{r}^{m-1}\mathtt{d}^{}$. Deleting a row we have $w^{-_\mathtt{r}}=\mathtt{w}\lambda^{-_\mathtt{r}})=\mathtt{d}^{}\mathtt{r}^{}  \mathtt{d}^{n-1}\mathtt{r}^{m-1}$ by Lemma \ref{rogs} (a).  A positive odd reflection gives 
$\mu=t_\alpha(\lambda^{-_\mathtt{r}})$ with $\mathtt{w}(\mu)=\mathtt{r}^{}  \mathtt{d}^{n}\mathtt{r}^{m-1}.$ Here $\alpha=\epsilon_1- \delta_1$ Then deleting a column we have $\mu^{-_\mathtt{c}}$ (which corresponds to the empty partition) by Lemma \ref{rogs} (c), and we have $\mathtt{w}(\mu^{-_\mathtt{c}})=\mathtt{d}^{n}\mathtt{r}^{m}$. Now by \eqref{1kr} 
$(\lambda,0)\sim (\lambda^{-_\mathtt{r}}, m)$. Then 
$(t_\alpha(\lambda^{-_\mathtt{r}}),m)=(\mu, m)$ 
and  by \eqref{2kr} 
$(\mu,m)\sim (\mu^{-_\mathtt{c}}, m+n)= (\emptyset, m+n)$.  
The same result is obtained by deleting a column first: we have
$\mathtt{w}(\lambda^{-_\mathtt{c}})=  \mathtt{d}^{n-1}\mathtt{r}^{m-1}\mathtt{d}\mathtt{r}$ by Lemma \ref{rogs}.  Then an  odd reflection using the root $\beta=\epsilon_n- \delta_m$ yields  
$\phi=r_\beta(\lambda^{-_\mathtt{c}})$, with $\mathtt{w}(\phi)= \mathtt{d}^{n-1}\mathtt{r}^{m}\mathtt{d}^{} .$ Then deleting a row we have $\mathtt{w}(\phi^{-_\mathtt{r}})=\mathtt{d}^{n}\mathtt{r}^{m}$.
 More generally if we carry out the same sequence of operations starting with a partition  $\xi$ containing  ${ \boldsymbol \lambda}, $ we obtain the skew diagram $\xi/{ \boldsymbol \lambda}$. This fits into the lower left corner of $X$. 
}

label: shg
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{shg}  If the functor $H$ satisfies Hypothesis \ref{ky}, then 
\begin{itemize} \item[{{\rm$($a$)$}}] There is a functor ${\mathbb H}:\mathfrak  T_{iso}\longrightarrow \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{X})$ given by ${\mathbb H}(\alpha) = \mathcal{X}_\alpha $ 
                  
and
\begin{equation} \label{syx}
{\mathbb H}(\rho_\alpha)[\lambda, in+jm] =
 [H(\rho_{\eta^{i}\nu^{j}\alpha})(\lambda),in+jm]
\mbox{ for  } (\lambda, in+jm)\in (X_{ \eta^{i}\nu^{j}\alpha},in+jm )                                 
.\end{equation}


\item[{{\rm$($b$)$}}] 
The injective map 
${\mathbb X}\longrightarrow \mathcal{X},$ $\lambda\longrightarrow [\lambda,0]$ is compatible with the 
 $\mathfrak T_{iso}$-action.  If 
$\lambda \in X_{\alpha}$, then ${\mathbb H}(\rho_{\alpha})[\lambda,0]= [H(\rho_{\alpha})(\lambda),0].$
\end{itemize}
Thus the action of 
 $\mathfrak T_{iso}$ on ${\mathbb X}$ extends to an action on $[{\mathbb X}\times Z].$

label: a12
title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Since $(\lambda,in+ jm)\sim  ({\lambda}^{-_\mathtt{r}},in+(j+1)m)$ and $(\lambda,in+ jm)\sim  ({\lambda}^{-_\mathtt{c}},(i+1)n+m)$ , to  show the action in \eqref{syx} is well-defined, by Lemma \ref{sogs} we need two conditions.

\begin{itemize} 
\item[{{\rm(i)}}] If 
$\lambda \in X_{ \eta^{i}\nu^{j}\alpha}$ and  ${\lambda}^{-_\mathtt{c}}\in X_{  \eta^{i+1}\nu^{j}\alpha}$ then
$$(H(\rho_{ \eta^{i} \nu^{j}\alpha})(\lambda),in+jm)\sim (H(\rho_{   \eta^{i+1}\nu^{j}\alpha})({\lambda}^{-_\mathtt{c}}),(i+1)n+jm).$$
\item[{{\rm(ii)}}] If 
$\lambda \in X_{ \eta^{i}\nu^{j}\alpha}$ and  ${\lambda}^{-_\mathtt{r}}\in X_{  \eta^{i}\nu^{j+1}\alpha}$ then
$$(H(\rho_{ \eta^{i} \nu^{j}\alpha})(\lambda),in+jm)\sim (H(\rho_{  \eta^{i}\nu^{j+1}\alpha})({\lambda}^{-_\mathtt{r}}),in+(j+1)m).$$

\end{itemize} For (i), set  $k= in+jm$ and  $\beta= \eta^{i}{ \nu^{j}\alpha}$, then
using the definition of $\sim$               
 and \eqref{kz1}
\begin{eqnarray} \label{a12}   
(H(\rho_{\beta})(\lambda),k)
&\sim& 
({H(\rho_{\beta})(\lambda)}^{-_\mathtt{c}},k+n)
\nonumber\\&=& 
(H(\rho_{\eta\beta})({\lambda}^{-_\mathtt{c}}),k+n).
\nonumber       
\end{eqnarray}  as required.  The proof of (ii) is similar using \eqref{kz}. 
In statement (b), injectivity of the map  ${\mathbb X}\longrightarrow [{\mathbb X}\times Z],$  follows from Corollary  \ref{vgs} (c) and the other statement follows from \eqref{syx} with $i=j=0$.

label: rhy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{rhy} If
$\lambda\in  X({\operatorname{r.full}})\cap  X_{\beta}$, then ${\lambda}^{-_\mathtt{r}} \in 
X_{\nu\beta}$,  ${t_{\beta}(\lambda)}\in X({\operatorname{r.full}})$ and  
\begin{equation} \label{kzt} {t_{\beta}(\lambda)}^{-_\mathtt{r}} = t_{\nu\beta}({\lambda}^{-_\mathtt{r}}).\end{equation}

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $\beta= \epsilon_i-\delta_{j}\in \Delta_{1}^+$ and set $t_\beta=   F(\rho_{\beta})$. 
Since $\lambda_1 = m$, $\lambda$ has no outer corners in row $\epsilon_{n}$. Thus 
                            
 $i<n$.
The equivalence of (a) and (b) in  Lemma \ref{rjx} implies 
$\nu\beta= \epsilon_{i+1}-\delta_j$  is an outer corner of ${\lambda}^{-_\mathtt{r}}$ and the rest follows from \eqref{qhf}.

label: ymn
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ymn} We have 
\begin{itemize} \item[{{\rm$($a$)$}}]
${\lambda}^{-_\mathtt{r}} =\zeta({\sigma}^{-_\mathtt{r}}).$
\item[{{\rm$($b$)$}}] ${\bf{sh}}(w)^{-_\mathtt{r}}= {\bf{sh}}(w^{-_\mathtt{r}})$, 
\item[{{\rm$($c$)$}}]  Suppose $\beta =\epsilon_i-\delta_j$ and                           
$r_{\beta}(\sigma) = (i,j')\sigma$ is obtained from $\sigma$ using the { odd reflection} $r_{\beta}$.
Then  
\begin{equation} \label{e6z}({r_\beta\sigma})^{-_\mathtt{r}}= r_{\nu\beta}({\sigma}^{-_\mathtt{r}}).\end{equation} 
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the first entry in ${ \boldsymbol \sigma}^{-_\mathtt{r}}$ is 1, the first step in the path corresponding
to $\zeta({\sigma}^{-_\mathtt{r}})$ is ${\operatorname{d}}$.        
For $i\ge 0$, step $i+1$ of this path is the same as 
step $i$ of the path for $\lambda$.  
This proves (a).
If $\mathtt{w}(\lambda)= \mathtt{x}\mathtt{d}$ and $\mathtt{w}(\lambda^{-_\mathtt{r}})= \mathtt{d}
\mathtt{x}$ as in Lemma \ref{rogs}, the same reasoning 
 gives (b). 
  For (c),  we use  (b), \eqref{kut} and Corollary \ref{APE}.  Thus 
$$r_{\beta}({\bf{sh}}(w))^{-_\mathtt{r}} = {\bf{sh}} (p_{\beta}(w))^{-_\mathtt{r}} = {\bf{sh}}(p_{\beta}(w)^{-_\mathtt{r}}) = {\bf{sh}}(p_{\nu\beta} (w^{-_\mathtt{r}})
=r_{\nu\beta}({\bf{sh}}(w^{-_\mathtt{r}})).$$

label: kps
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{kps}  If $E_{j} = \{(w_i,k_i)| i \in \mathcal{E}_{j}\},$ then  $E = \bigcup_{i=0}^{m-1} E_j$ is the decomposition of $E$ into $\approx$-equivalence classes.
head: environment

label: ops
title: Proof
body_md:
Define a  map $f:\{0,1,\ldots m+n-1\} \longrightarrow {\mathbb Z}_m$ so that $f(i)$ is minimal with $i\in \mathcal{E}_{f(i)}$. 
By \eqref{ips}  
\begin{equation} \label{ops}  k_{i+1} = k_i +nc_{i+1} -md_{i+1}. 
\end{equation}
Note that the $i+1^{st}$ entry in $w_0$ equals the first entry in $w_i$.  There are two cases
\begin{itemize} \item[{{\rm$($a$)$}}]  $w_i = \mathtt{r}\mathtt{x}$ for some word $\mathtt{x}$ and $c_{i+1} =1.$  Then 
 $k_{i+1} = k_i +n$ and so $f(i+1) =f(i) +1$.
\item[{{\rm$($b$)$}}] $w_i = \mathtt{d}\mathtt{x}$ for some word $\mathtt{x}$ and $c_{i+1} =0$.  Then 
 $k_{i+1} = k_i \mod m$ and thus $f(i+1) =f(i).$
\end{itemize}  Also $f$ is onto since $w$ contains $m$ letters equal to $\mathtt{r}.$ Hence each $E_j$ is  non-empty.  
It follows from (b) that each $E_{j}$ is  a union  of $\approx$-equivalence classes.  Also if $ (w_i,k_i)\approx
 (w_\ell,k_\ell)$ then $m$ divides $k_\ell-k_i$.  Thus the $E_j$ are precisely  the  $\approx$-equivalence classes.
head: environment

label: vgt
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{vgt} 
\begin{itemize} \item[{}]  \item[{{\rm$($a$)$}}]
$E$  contains a representative of the form $(w,\ell)$
such that $m$ divides $\ell$.                                                
\item[{{\rm$($b$)$}}] The set of representatives as in (a) forms an  equivalence class of   under $\approx.$ 
\item[{{\rm$($c$)$}}]  Suppose that $(w_0, k_0)$ has the property in (a), and                            
$[w_0, k_0] \longrightarrow p [w_0, k_0]$ is a positive edge  of the Cayley graph $\Gamma[\mathtt{W}\times {\mathbb Z}]$  then $p$ has a representative of the form $(w_0, k_0)\longrightarrow (p_\gamma (w_0), k_0)$ or $(w_0, k_0)\longrightarrow (p_\gamma (w_0), k_0+m)$. 
                                                                           
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Given $(w_0,k_0)$ solve $k_0+nj \equiv 0 \mod m$ for $j$. Then if $i \in \mathcal{E}_j$, $k_i\equiv 0$ mod $m$.   This gives (a) and (b) follows from \eqref{ips}.  
                                                                                                                             
                                                                                    
\\ \\
The  hypotheses in (c) implies that for some $j$ and  root $\beta\in\Delta_1^+$, $w_j=R^{j}(w_0) \in W(\beta)$, see \eqref{inb} for notation. Then 
$\beta$ corresponds to a consecutive pair $\mathtt{d} \mathtt{r}$ in $w_j$ in entries $k, k+1$: 
$$ w_j=y_1y_2, \ldots y_{m+n}$$
 with $y_{k} = \mathtt{d},     y_{k+1}=\mathtt{r}$.  In $w_0=R^{-j}(w_j),$ there is another consecutive pair $\mathtt{d} \mathtt{r}$  in entries $k+j, k+j+1$. Unless 
$w=\mathtt{r} u \mathtt{d} $ 
and $k+j\equiv m+n \mod m+n$,  this pair yields a root $\alpha\in\Delta_1^+$ such that 
$w_0 \in W(\alpha)$.  Let $w'_0=p_\alpha(w_0)$ and $w'_j=p_\beta(w_j)$.  Then $w'_j=R^{j}(w'_0)$  and $(w'_0, k_0)\sim (w'_j,k_j)$.   Then $p$ is represented by $(w_0, k_0) \longrightarrow  ({p_{\alpha}(w_0)},k)$.                                                             
 In the exceptional case where 
$w=\mathtt{r} u \mathtt{d} $ 
and $k+j\equiv m+n \mod m+n$,    ${ \boldsymbol \lambda} \subseteq  \lambda$  and 
$\alpha =\epsilon_n-\delta_1$ is an outer pseudocorner of $\lambda$ as in   Lemma \ref{rey}.  Then  by Equation \eqref{1no}, $p$ is represented by $(w_0, k_0) \longrightarrow  ({p_{\gamma}(w_0^{-_\mathtt{r}})},k+m)$ where $\gamma = \nu \alpha$.
head: environment

label: vss
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{vss} 
There is  a  
$\mathfrak T_{{\operatorname{iso}}}$-equivariant bijection $[X\times m{\mathbb Z}]_\approx \longrightarrow [X\times {\mathbb Z}]$ given by
$$[\lambda,  m\ell]_\approx \longrightarrow [\lambda,  m\ell].$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The map is well-defined because $e\approx e'$ implies $e\sim e'$ and is clearly 
$\mathfrak T_{{\operatorname{iso}}}$-equivariant.  It is onto by Lemma \ref{vgt}. To show it is injective, suppose $ m\ell =k_0$ and the pairs $(\lambda,  m\ell)$ and $(w_{0},k_{0})$ correspond under the bijection $(X\times {\mathbb Z}) \longleftrightarrow (\mathtt{W}\times {\mathbb Z})$. 
The equivalence class of $(w_{0},k_{0})$ is the set $E$ from Corollary \ref{vgs} (a).                                                             
If  $(\lambda,  m\ell)\sim (\mu,  mr)$, then $(\mu,  mr)$  
corresponds to  a pair $(w_{i},k_{i})$ such that $m$ divides $k_i -k_0$.  Hence $(w_{0},k_{0})\approx (w_{i},k_{i})$ by Corollary \ref{vgs} (d) and the result follows.
head: environment

label: E3
title: Example
body_md:
\label{E3}{\rm                                            
 Let $(n,m) =(2,3)$.  The Hasse diagrams for $[X\times m{\mathbb Z}]_\approx$  and $[X\times {\mathbb Z}]$ 
are isomorphic by Theorem \ref{vss}.  
We give the portion of the Hasse diagram of  $[X\times 3{\mathbb Z}] $ in degrees 0-6.
  The rotation number $k$ is given as a superscript and is omitted if $k=0$.   The degree, as defined in \eqref{e67n}  is given in the last row. Because of the periodic nature of this poset, the part in degree $i+6$ is obtained  from the degree $i$ part by increasing the rotation number by 6. So the portion below determines the entire graph.   
\begin{equation*}
                               
\xymatrix@C=1pc@R=1pc{\emptyset\ar@{->}[r] &
\ydiagram{1}\ar@{->}[ddr]&
\ydiagram{1,1} \ar@{<-}[l] \ar@{->}[r]& \ydiagram{0+1,2}\ar@{->}[r] \ar@{->}[ddr]   &
\ydiagram{2,2} \ar@{->}[r]&\ydiagram{0+2,3} \ar@{->}[r] \ar@{->}[ddr]& \ydiagram{3,3}=\emptyset^{6}\ar@{->}[r]&
                             
\\ \\
             
 \ydiagram{0+1,2}^{-3}\ar@{->}[r] \ar@{->}[uur]&\ydiagram{2,2}^{-3}\ar@{->}[r]&
\ydiagram{2}\ar@{<-}[l] \ar@{->}[r] \ar@{->}[uur]&\ydiagram{3}\ar@{->}[r]&
\ydiagram{0+1,3}\ar@{->}[r] \ar@{->}[uur]&\ydiagram{1,1}^3\ar@{->}[r]& \ydiagram{0+1,2}^3\ar@{->}[r]\ar@{->}[uur]&\\
0&1&2&3&4&5&6}
\end{equation*}
           
 The most interesting behavior occurs when the rotation number changes after a morphism is applied.  Here are some examples                               
By  \eqref{1no}                   
we obtain 
                                                                                    
\begin{equation} \label{sb1}{\mathbb F}(\rho_{\epsilon_2 -\delta_1})[(3,i),0)]=[t_{\epsilon_1 -\delta_1}(i,0),3] =[((i,1),{3})]=[(i,1)^{3}] \mbox{ for } i=1,2.\end{equation}
Together with the more obvious morphism $(1,1)^3 \longrightarrow (2,1)^3$, this accounts for the extra arrows in the lower right that do not appear in the Hasse diagram for the poset $X$.
                                                                             
                                                                                
Using   \eqref{2no} 
$${\mathbb F}(\rho_{\delta_3-\epsilon_1})[(i,0),0)]={\mathbb F}(\rho_{\delta_3-\epsilon_1})[(3,i),{-3})]=[t_{\delta_3-\epsilon_2 }(3,i),{-3}]  =[(2,i)^{-3}]  \mbox{ for } i=1,2.$$     
The diagram shows only positive morphisms, but the last equation is equivalent to
$${\mathbb F}(\rho_{\epsilon_1-\delta_3})[(2,i)^{-3}] =[(i,0),0)] \mbox{ for } i=1,2.$$
This accounts for the  extra arrows in the lower left  of the diagram.  In general the proof of Lemma \ref{vgt} shows that the arrows that do not appear in the Hasse diagram for  $X$ arise from pseudocorners.
}

label: crb
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{crb} There is well defined an equivariant bijection $x:{[\stackrel{{\rm o}}
{\mathcal{B}}} \times {\mathbb Z}] \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}$ where $[{\stackrel{{\rm o}}{\mathfrak{b}}}{}(\sigma),k]$  maps to the Borel subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}$ extended from ${\stackrel{{\rm o}}{\mathfrak{b}}}{}(\sigma,k)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the equivalence relation $\sim$ is generated by \eqref{1kr}  and \eqref{2kr},  to show $x$ is well-defined, it is enough to check the following 
\begin{itemize} \item[{{\rm$($a$)$}}]  
If $\lambda \in X({\operatorname{r.full}})$ the Borel subalgebras ${\stackrel{{\rm o}}{\mathfrak{b}}}{}(\lambda^{-_\mathtt{r}},k+m)$ and ${\stackrel{{\rm o}}{\mathfrak{b}}}{}(\lambda,k)$
 extend to the same Borel subalgebra of $\widehat{L}(\stackrel{{\rm _o}}{\mathfrak{g}})$.
\item[{{\rm$($b$)$}}]  
If  $\lambda \in X({\operatorname{c.empty}})$ the Borel subalgebras ${\stackrel{{\rm o}}{\mathfrak{b}}}{}(\lambda^{+_\mathtt{c}},k-n)$ and ${\stackrel{{\rm o}}{\mathfrak{b}}}{}(\lambda,k)$
 extend to the same Borel subalgebra of $\widehat{L}(\stackrel{{\rm _o}}{\mathfrak{g}})$.
\end{itemize}  This is straightforward.
Note that equivariance follows from Lemma \ref{ymn} and the remarks earlier in this Subsection. 
The map ${x:[\stackrel{{\rm o}}{\mathcal{B}}} \times {\mathbb Z}] \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}$ is onto by definition of $\mathcal{B}$.  To show it is injective, suppose
$x[\stackrel{\rm o}{\mathfrak{b}}(w,k)] =\mathfrak{b}$.  Then 
DK diagram $D$ for $\mathfrak{b}$ determines a set of $m+n$ words $w_i$ as in Subsection \ref{dta}, see  also Example \ref{iob}.
                
                                                                               
Any Borel  that extends to $\mathfrak{b}$ has a diagram obtaained by deleting a node from $D$. But we have shown in Corollary \ref{vgs} that the equivalence class of $\stackrel{\rm o}{\mathfrak{b}}(w_0,k_0)$ has size $m+n$ and consists of the set $\{\stackrel{\rm o}{\mathfrak{b}}(w_i,k_i)| 0 \le  i < m+n\}.$  
                           
Therefore the preimage of $\mathfrak{b}$ under $x$ consists of this single equivalence class.
